Chapter 7—Navigating Obstacles: Dealing with Restlessness, Boredom, and Doubt
So, even when you set out with the best intentions, mindfulness practice isn’t always a smooth ride, is it? You might run into some familiar roadblocks—like feeling restless, bored, sleepy, or even doubting whether you’re doing it right. And when these pop up, it’s totally normal to feel like throwing in the towel.
But here’s something important to remember: obstacles aren’t a sign you’re failing. They’re just a natural part of learning. Every time you face one, it’s actually a chance to grow your patience and deepen your understanding.
Let’s walk through some of the common challenges you might bump into:
First up, restlessness. Ever notice your mind jumping from thought to thought, or your body feeling fidgety? Instead of wrestling with that energy or trying to push it away, mindfulness is about noticing what’s really happening. Maybe your legs feel buzzy, or your thoughts are racing. Just acknowledge it, and then gently bring your attention back to your breath or your body.
Then there’s boredom. Sometimes, practice can seem dull or like you’re just repeating the same thing. But what if you got curious instead of distracted? Try asking yourself, “What does boredom feel like in my body right now?” Sometimes, you’ll discover subtle sensations or emotions hiding just beneath the surface.
Sleepiness is another common visitor, especially when things get quiet. If you notice yourself getting drowsy, meet it with kindness. Maybe open your eyes, shift your posture, or even try standing meditation for a change of pace.
And of course, there’s doubt. Thoughts like, “I’m not doing this right,” or “This isn’t working for me” show up for everyone. When they do, you can simply label them as “doubting”—and watch them come and go like any other thought, with gentle awareness.
Here’s an analogy I love: imagine mindfulness as tending a garden. Sometimes, weeds—these obstacles—will sprout up. Instead of ignoring them or getting frustrated, you just notice them, understand what they are, and gently work with them. Over time, your garden grows stronger and more vibrant.
Now, what can you actually do when these obstacles show up?
Sometimes, it helps to shorten your practice. On tough days, even a few mindful breaths or a quick body scan can be enough.
Or maybe you need to change your focus. If sitting feels tough, try mindful walking or gentle movement to refresh your attention.
And don’t forget about connecting with others. Sharing your experiences with a friend or mindfulness group can offer encouragement and a fresh perspective.
By meeting these obstacles with patience and a flexible attitude, your practice gets easier, more sustainable, and honestly, a lot more rewarding.
